guides.content:
# libtmux for Elixir
An Elixir library for controlling tmux. The core provides exact target references, shared deadlines, command encoding, bounded protocol parsing, Linux one-shot execution, immutable graph capture, Enumerable selections and portable filters. The domain client API remains under development. [Contributing](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) · [First task](docs/first-task.md) · [Design](docs/design.md) · [Encoding](docs/encoding.md) · [Mental model](docs/mental-model.md) · [Observations](docs/observations.md) · [Filtering](docs/filtering.md) · [Ownership](docs/ownership.md) · [Writing](.github/WRITING.md) · [Artwork](docs/branding.md) ## Status and requirements | Component | Current scope | | --- | --- | | Mix application | `:libtmux`, version `0.0.1-alpha.1` | | Development toolchain | Elixir `1.20.x` (at least `1.20.4`) on Erlang/OTP `29.x` | | Planned tmux floor | `3.3`; fixture checks precede client compatibility qualification | | Runtime dependencies | No third-party packages; own native I/O helper | | Platforms | No runtime support matrix has been qualified | [`.tool-versions`](.tool-versions) selects the development toolchain ranges for mise and CI. Linux builds require a C11 compiler for the helper. See [setup](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md#setup) for installation and upgrades. tmux is not required for the pure checks. Capture, command execution and the complete example require an external tmux executable. The supported client API and compatibility matrix remain under qualification. ## Installation Add the alpha release to your Mix dependencies: ```elixir {:libtmux, "== 0.0.1-alpha.1"} ``` Fetch dependencies: ```console $ mix deps.get ``` ## Capture, select and execute From a source checkout, run the complete public API example from the packed core on a new isolated tmux server. This requires Linux, a C11 compiler, Python 3 and tmux 3.3 or newer: ```console $ MIX_ENV=test mix run scripts/check_package.exs --examples ``` The example captures one graph, selects its active pane, and reads that exact pane through one-shot and control commands. It checks the acknowledged result, retires its connection, and verifies owned server cleanup. The check uses a temporary socket and empty configuration. See the [complete program and failure behavior](docs/first-task.md). ## Check the implementation From the checkout, with the development toolchain on `PATH`, check formatting: ```console $ mix format --check-formatted ``` Run the pure unit suite: ```console $ mix test ``` Compile with warnings treated as errors: ```console $ mix compile --warnings-as-errors ``` With Hex installed, build a local package archive: ```console $ mix hex.build ``` Check public core imports from a packed archive outside the checkout: ```console $ mix run scripts/check_package.exs ``` The unit and packed-core checks validate the current foundations. Real integration checks cover owned startup/teardown and hostile command/format bytes through real tmux. They do not qualify the future client API or a complete compatibility matrix. See [Contributing](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) for setup, timing budgets, and the checks required as implementation arrives. ## Planned package boundaries The core provides immutable observations and explicit tmux operations, using Elixir and OTP without third-party runtime dependencies. Workspace loading and an MCP server have separate Mix projects under `packages/`. Their runtime implementations remain planned. MCP also consumes workspace behavior rather than maintaining a second loader or planner. The [design note](docs/design.md) records these boundaries and the contracts that implementation must prove. It is not an API reference. ## Contributing and references Follow the [contribution guide](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [writing guide](.github/WRITING.md). Agent instructions start in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). Related projects: [libtmux for Python](https://github.com/tmux-python/libtmux), [libtmux ports](https://github.com/libtmux), and [tmux](https://github.com/tmux/tmux). Licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE).

# Filter captured values

Obtain one [snapshot](observations.md), then select its observed panes:

```elixir
alias LibTmux.{Selection, Snapshot}

editors =
  snapshot
  |> Snapshot.panes()
  |> Selection.where(active: true, current_command: [in: ["nvim", "vim"]])

Enum.map(editors, & &1.id)
```

Selections retain their immutable graph and order. Enumerable delegates to
the materialized list, including suspension and early halt. `size/1` uses
the cached count; ordinary `Enum.member?/2` compares elements. Use
`Selection.member_id?/2` for native ID membership. Enumeration performs no I/O.

`Selection.filter/2` accepts only unary functions and uses Enum truthiness.
Predicate exceptions propagate. `where/2` accepts validated data: keywords
are shorthand for maps, with duplicate keys rejected at every nesting level.
Both validate before scanning, including when no items remain.

`one/2` returns `{:ok, item}` or a structured `:no_match` / `:multiple_matches`
error. `one_or_nil/2` permits zero matches. Their bang variants raise the
same error; both stop at the second match. `exists?/2` stops at its first
match. `count/2` counts matching items; `size/1` returns the cached total.

## Predicate grammar

A bare scalar means equality. Explicit `%{equals: value}` is equivalent.
The [generated schema](schema.md) lists each field's type and operators.
Numbers compare numerically, strings compare case-sensitively without
normalization, and nullable numeric ordering against known nil is false.
`not` negates equality; `not_in` negates membership, including known nil.
Portable regex is not supported. Native predicates may use `Regex` directly.

Fields in one object conjoin. Boolean `and` and `or` accept lists of
criteria; `not` accepts one criteria object. Empty `and` is true and empty
`or` is false. Normalization never combines separate relation quantifiers:

```elixir
Selection.where(Snapshot.sessions(snapshot), %{
  panes: %{some: %{active: true, current_command: "nvim"}}
})
```

That predicate requires one pane to satisfy both conditions. Two separate
`some` clauses can match different panes. `every` and `none` are true for
a known-empty relation; `some` is false. `count` counts that relation's
identities: physical windows/panes deduplicate, window links retain memberships.

To-one `is: criteria` is false for known absence and `is_not` negates it.
`is: nil` means absent; `is_not: nil` means present. Session `active_window`
is derived from a complete link domain and loaded active flags. Zero active
links means known absence; multiple active links raise `:ambiguous_relation`.
An unresolved active target remains unloaded. Coverage checks run before
evaluation, including fields behind a Boolean branch that cannot match.

## External filters

`Filter.new/3` returns a validated portable value, and `new!/3` raises its
structured error. Applying that value retains its constructor validation;
explicit new limits validate the normalized tree without generating extra
criteria objects. Prepared predicates may contain
sets and closures; portable filters contain data only.

`Filter.from_json/3` uses built-in JSON and rejects duplicate keys before
map conversion, trailing data and unknown names. `from_wire/3` accepts an
already decoded map; that map cannot reveal discarded duplicate keys.
Neither decoder creates atoms from external keys. Encode through
`Filter.to_wire/1`, then `JSON.encode!/1`.

```json
{"version":1,"entity":"pane","where":{"active":true,"currentCommand":{"in":["nvim","vim"]}}}
```

Default ceilings are 65,536 bytes, depth 16, 1024 value nodes, 256 array
elements and 8192 bytes per string. Wire depth starts at root zero and
counts every member/element; the ceiling is inclusive. Positive integer
options `max_bytes`, `max_depth`, `max_nodes`, `max_list` and
`max_string_bytes` can narrow or widen the constructor budget. JSON object
members have a fixed ceiling of 256. Native input depth counts criteria
objects and also bounds the normalized tree. A normalized conjunction does
not add relation/Boolean nesting; disjunctions, negations and relation
children do. Wire budgets additionally cover the full versioned envelope.
Errors carry the affected path, including Boolean and membership indexes;
early parser-limit errors can identify the root before a path is available.

Selections and filters operate on captured values. Server query planning
and pushdown remain under implementation.

# Capture a pane and read it through both transports

From a source checkout, run one complete example against an isolated tmux
server:

```console
$ MIX_ENV=test mix run scripts/check_package.exs --examples
```

Use the development toolchain and Linux prerequisites in
[Contributing](../.github/CONTRIBUTING.md#setup), plus Python 3 and tmux 3.3 or
newer on `PATH`. Set `LIBTMUX_TMUX` to an absolute executable when checking a
particular tmux build. Hex must already be installed; the check downloads
nothing.

The check builds and extracts a real package, compiles its core in a fresh
directory, and executes the packaged example outside the checkout. An owned
fixture supplies a unique socket, empty configuration and existing session.
It clears inherited `TMUX` and `TMUX_PANE` and verifies its server, pane,
clients and helper exit afterward. It never uses the default server.

## The complete program

[Executable source](../examples/capture_and_read.exs) receives the absolute
tmux executable, socket and existing session ID from that fixture. All its
library calls use the public core. The embedded program is checked against
that source file.

<!-- example: examples/capture_and_read.exs -->

```elixir
alias LibTmux.{Codec, Command, Control, Format, Operation, Ref, Selection, Server, Snapshot}
alias LibTmux.Control.Request

[executable, socket, session_id] = System.argv()
{:ok, _} = Application.ensure_all_started(:libtmux)

server =
  Server.new(
    executable: executable,
    socket: socket,
    cwd: "/",
    env: Map.drop(System.get_env(), ["TMUX", "TMUX_PANE"])
  )

{:ok, snapshot} = Server.snapshot(server)
session = snapshot |> Snapshot.sessions() |> Selection.one!(id: session_id)
window = Snapshot.related(snapshot, :session, session.id, :active_window)

pane =
  snapshot
  |> Snapshot.panes()
  |> Selection.where(window_id: window.id)
  |> Selection.filter(& &1.active)
  |> Selection.one!()

{:ok, target} = Ref.new(:pane, pane.id, snapshot.server_instance)
command = Command.new("display-message", ["-p", "-t", pane.id, Format.field("pane_id")])
{:ok, %{stdout: stdout, cleanup: :retired}} = Server.run(server, command)
{:ok, one_shot_id} = Codec.decode_field(stdout, :string, encoding: :escaped_v1)
true = one_shot_id == pane.id

{:ok, root, control} =
  Control.start_link(
    server: server,
    session: {:existing, session.id},
    lane: :host_qualified,
    timeout: 800
  )

root_monitor = Process.monitor(root)

control_id =
  try do
    {:ok, operation} = Control.submit(control, Request.field("pane_id", target), timeout: 800)

    {:ok,
     %{
       outcome: :completed,
       certainty: :acknowledged,
       evidence: :command_reply,
       lines: [line]
     }} = Operation.await(operation, timeout: 800)

    {:ok, id} = Codec.decode_field(line <> "\n", :string, encoding: :escaped_v1)
    true = id == pane.id
    id
  after
    try do
      :ok = Control.close(control, timeout: 800)
    after
      :ok = Supervisor.stop(root, :normal, 800)

      receive do
        {:DOWN, ^root_monitor, :process, ^root, :normal} -> :ok
      after
        800 -> raise "connection supervisor did not exit"
      end
    end
  end

IO.puts(
  JSON.encode!(%{
    "session" => session.id,
    "window" => window.id,
    "pane" => pane.id,
    "oneShot" => one_shot_id,
    "control" => control_id,
    "connectionRetired" => true
  })
)
```

<!-- /example -->

The result contains the observed session, window and pane IDs. Both replies
must identify the selected pane, and `connectionRetired` is true only after
connection close and supervisor exit succeed. The harness checks that the
borrowed server and pane survived the program, then tears down its own fixture.

## What each step establishes

`LibTmux.Server.snapshot/2` observes a capture interval. `LibTmux.Selection`
then runs `where`, a native predicate and checked cardinality locally, without
another tmux command. Relationships resolve against the same graph. Keep
using that snapshot when several decisions need the same captured values.

The one-shot read uses an exact pane ID and the escaped field codec. Its
check/use race remains: a captured pane is not reserved. The control request
also carries a `LibTmux.Ref` bound to the observed server incarnation.

Control startup explicitly attaches a client and can change session state
and attachment counts. The fixture's empty, controlled configuration is why
this example can declare `lane: :host_qualified`. A caller using another
server must qualify its effective hooks, aliases and stream writers before
using that lane; the option does not perform that qualification.

`LibTmux.Control.submit/3` returns an admitted operation. The example checks
the result of `LibTmux.Operation.await/2` for both `:completed` and
`:acknowledged`. A reply acknowledges this tmux command; it does not prove
that an arbitrary program started by another command has exited.

## Failure behavior and cleanup

The program uses assertions so unexpected results make the example fail.
Capture and transport errors return `{:error, %LibTmux.Error{}}`, with `kind`,
`phase` and `certainty` describing the failure. A control field read whose
target disappeared returns an acknowledged `:failed` operation; a present
empty field remains `:completed`. Raw one-shot commands retain tmux's native
semantics, so the example also checks the returned pane ID. Neither path
retries with a positional target.
`LibTmux.Selection.one!/2` raises `:no_match` or `:multiple_matches` rather
than selecting arbitrarily.

An await API timeout ends only that waiter. Canonical failed, skipped and
unknown operation outcomes are values, including from bang methods. Inspect
the retained operation instead of replaying an uncertain command. This
example deliberately accepts only an acknowledged completed read.

The `after` block closes the connection and stops its enclosing supervisor.
The separate fixture harness runs owned teardown even when the example
fails. See [the mental model](mental-model.md) and
[ownership](ownership.md) for the different lifetimes and remaining runtime
qualification limits.

# Read values, execute explicitly

Capture once when several decisions should use the same observed graph.
Keep that snapshot while selecting and filtering. Execute a new command
explicitly when you need another observation or an effect.
Capture records an interval; fields can change during it. The resulting
value stays fixed while live objects continue changing.

## The values you hold

| Value | What it represents | I/O boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LibTmux.Server` | Executable, socket and environment for an existing server | Pure descriptor construction |
| `LibTmux.Snapshot` | An indexed graph captured over one interval | `LibTmux.Server.snapshot/2` captures a new value |
| `LibTmux.Selection` | Ordered items and their originating snapshot | Filtering and enumeration use captured values |
| `LibTmux.Ref` | An observed exact ID and server instance | Pure identity data; it reserves nothing |
| `LibTmux.Control` | A handle pinned to one connection epoch | Status reads are local; startup explicitly attaches a client |
| `LibTmux.Operation` | Access to one retained operation record | Result/status reads are local; awaiting registers a separate waiter |

Windows are physical objects. `LibTmux.WindowLink` supplies their membership
in a session, index and active state. A linked window can appear more than
once while its panes remain the same physical panes. Choose window links
when membership matters; choose panes when an action should address each
physical pane once. See [captured state](observations.md).

## Coverage tells you which questions the graph can answer

A loaded field may contain a value, an empty string or a documented `nil`.
`:unloaded` means this snapshot does not contain the observation.
`:unavailable` means the capability is absent. Neither means known absence.

Relationship predicates need complete captured join domains. A missing pane
relation cannot satisfy “no pane matches.” Validation raises a structured
coverage error before filtering, including an empty selection. Obtain a new
snapshot explicitly when more coverage is needed. Existing selections retain
their original graph. See [filtering](filtering.md).

## Server identity and connection epochs have different lifetimes

A server instance identifies one tmux process incarnation. Native object IDs
can be reused after that process exits. References retain the observed
instance so qualified control requests can reject known stale targets.
One-shot commands retain a check/use race; an observed ID reserves nothing.

An epoch identifies one control connection and its owned transport actors.
`LibTmux.Control.reconnect/2` obtains the ready epoch and returns it unchanged
when it is already ready. Close first to require a replacement. Replacement
waits for retirement and returns a new pinned handle. The server instance
can stay the same while the epoch changes. Old connection handles cannot
submit into the replacement. Reconnect never replays work.

## Waiting, command outcomes and retirement are separate

| Result | What the caller can conclude |
| --- | --- |
| `LibTmux.Control.submit/3` returns `{:ok, operation}` | Admission succeeded; inspect or await the retained operation |
| `LibTmux.Operation.await/2` returns an API timeout | This waiter ended; the operation may still advance |
| A canonical outcome is `:completed` or `:failed` with `:acknowledged` certainty | tmux supplied a command reply; arbitrary programs started by that command have their own lifetimes |
| A canonical outcome is `:skipped` with `:no_write` certainty | The operation was classified before dispatch |
| A canonical outcome is `:unknown` | Available evidence cannot determine its effects |
| Operation status reports `wire: :retired` | Reply attribution has retired; the retained record may still occupy capacity |
| `LibTmux.Control.close/2` returns `:ok` | The pinned connection epoch retired; its enclosing supervisor remains running |

Each await call has its own budget. Timeout or caller death ends that waiter
without cancelling the operation. For wire-active work,
`LibTmux.Operation.stop/1` requests closure of the entire pinned epoch and can
affect siblings. An already retired operation returns `:ok` without closing
its connection. Use `LibTmux.Control.close/2` to wait for connection retirement.
Inspect retained results instead of replaying an uncertain mutation.

Once a canonical outcome exists, it stays unchanged. Bang operation APIs
raise API/context errors and still return canonical failed, skipped and
unknown outcomes as values. Wire retirement, record expiry and native process
cleanup each have their own evidence. See [ownership](ownership.md) for
deadlines, bounds and the remaining qualification limits.

# Captured tmux state

`LibTmux.Server.new/1` constructs a descriptor with an explicit executable
and socket. It performs no I/O. `LibTmux.Server.snapshot/2` observes that
existing server and returns an immutable `LibTmux.Snapshot`. Neither call
attaches a control client or starts a missing server. Configured tmux hooks
remain environmental effects of commands, including list commands.

## Read one captured graph

`Snapshot.items/2` returns a plain list for an entity atom or module.
`Snapshot.fetch/3` looks up an exact ID. `Snapshot.related/4` follows captured
indexes and raises a structured coverage error when a relation is incomplete.
These functions perform no I/O. `Snapshot.sessions/1`, `windows/1`, `panes/1`,
`window_links/1` and `clients/1` return materialized Enumerable selections.
See [filtering](filtering.md) for local predicates and portable criteria.

Sessions, physical windows, panes and clients have separate maps. A pane
belongs to one physical window. `WindowLink` records session membership,
window index and active state. Its key includes session ID, index and window
ID; it does not prove a unique lifetime after unlink and relink.

A window can appear at multiple indexes in the same session and in other
sessions. Server-wide physical maps deduplicate identical rows and reject
conflicting rows. Session pane traversal returns each physical pane once;
window-link traversal preserves memberships. Session/window/pane lists sort
by numeric native ID. Links sort by numeric session ID and index; clients
sort bytewise by their validated observed names.

`Session.attached_count` preserves tmux's raw client count. `attached` is
derived from that count. Explicit control clients remain counted even with
`no-output` and `ignore-size`. A control client's height is known `nil` when
tmux reports no started tty; it is not an unavailable field.

## Coverage and construction

`Snapshot.new/2` validates fixture or adapter observations without I/O.
`fields` declares loaded fields over the supplied entity IDs. `complete`
declares complete server entity sets; omissions remain partial. `unavailable`
declares absent capabilities separately. Declared names and values validate
before indexes or relations become observable.

Known empty strings, known nullable values, `:unloaded` and `:unavailable`
remain distinct. Required coverage checks run even for empty entity sets.
Derived attachment coverage follows its source count. A relation to many
objects needs a complete join domain, so missing children never become an
empty relation. Complete target sets reject dangling references. A partial
target set can retain unresolved foreign IDs, but traversal fails explicitly.

The [generated schema](schema.md) owns field types, explicit wire names,
tmux variables and relation cardinalities. Physical windows carry no single
session, session index or active membership flag.

## Capture consistency and bounds

Capture reads topology, then named fields, then topology again. It checks
the tmux PID against Linux boot identity and process start ticks before and
after those reads. Replacement or changing references trigger finite read
retries. A disappearing read target can retry; invalid encoding and other
decoding errors remain visible. Two attempts are the default; one to three
may be requested. All attempts share one deadline and the original budgets.

Defaults are 1024 contextual entity rows, 512 commands, 8 MiB total response
bytes, 64 KiB per response and 5000 ms. Both stdout and stderr, including
failed-command output, consume the byte budget. Overload returns an error
instead of a truncated success. Topology checks and retries also consume
work. One-shot retirement has the separate allowance documented in
[ownership](ownership.md).

Free-form fields use the qualified versioned encoder. Numeric/ID topology
columns validate their complete representation. Client rows combine one
encoded identity with restricted scalar columns; tabs and newlines cannot
escape the encoded identity. This is a fixed capture schema, not a general
raw-format row parser.

The capture interval records observation, not a transaction. Attributes can
change within it; matching topology before and after does not prove nothing
changed in between. Holding a snapshot reserves no objects. Its server
instance is distinct from a future connection epoch, and one-shot checks
retain a check/use race. Sending snapshots between BEAM processes can copy
terms; retaining one can retain its graph.

# One-shot process ownership

`LibTmux.Transport.OneShot.run/3` runs an absolute executable and argv on
Linux without a shell. It returns bytes, process exit status and cleanup
evidence separately. A nonzero process exit is still a completed transport
result; the tmux command layer must interpret that status. The domain
client and public persistent transport remain under implementation.

The native helper supplies receive credits that an ordinary OTP Port
lacks. It reads each stdout/stderr pipe only against one bounded credit;
its control pipe stays responsive while output or stdin is blocked. A
capture limit after delivery cannot bound an upstream mailbox while its
owner is descheduled.

## Limits and results

Default ceilings are 1 MiB stdout, 64 KiB stderr and 4096 retained chunks.
Byte limits may be 0–16 MiB per stream; chunk limits may be 1–65,536.
`max_total_bytes` limits both streams together to 0–32 MiB; its default is
the sum of the stream limits. The retained prefix obeys both ceilings.
Encoded cwd, argv and environment together fit a 32 KiB initialization
payload. Argv and environment each have at most 256 entries, including
argv's executable. Target environment values preserve empty strings and
non-NUL bytes; inherited tmux context is removed. Requested variables apply
to child `execve`; the helper inherits the trusted host environment.

The timeout defaults to 5000 ms and is at most 600,000 ms. A caller can
pass an existing `LibTmux.Deadline` instead. Admission, startup and capture
share that budget. Cleanup has a separate allowance up to 750 ms. Expiry
never turns partial output into success.

Overload stops the owned producer and returns a structured error with a
bounded prefix. `cleanup: :retired` requires private child-retirement evidence
and helper exit. Missing proof stays `:unknown`. An exit status or retryable
error never authorizes replay.

The worker acknowledges terminal child-retirement proof before the helper
exits. The helper keeps its input open while earlier cancellation or read
credits drain; after acknowledgement the worker writes nothing further.
This preserves the helper's separate exit-status evidence. Missing
acknowledgement uses the existing 750 ms delivery allowance.

The worker monitors its caller. Caller death initiates cleanup; worker/VM
death closes the helper's parent pipe. Caller settlement and retirement
remain separate. Closing the reply alias also removes an already-delivered
result, releasing captured bytes from the caller's mailbox.

## Accounting and scope

Per-call bounds cover output bytes, chunk metadata, encoded input and
private frames. Captured chunks can coexist with an assembled result;
account for both copies. The helper has fixed input, queue and write
buffers and bounded initialization allocations. It requests 8 KiB child
pipes and a 4 KiB signal pipe. Kernel page rounding can increase the actual
capacities; a resize failure rejects startup. Parent pipes and Port delivery add
buffers outside the capture byte count. Aggregate accounting must measure
actual pipe capacities. See [the protocol](../c_src/README.md).

This primitive has one request per worker and no shared request queue.
Applications creating many independent callers need admission limits at
their host/server boundary. A per-call ceiling is not a global memory
ceiling. Ordinary finite descendants are killed and reaped. Uninterruptible
tasks, helper SIGKILL, hostile escape and host compromise are outside that
guarantee; incomplete cleanup retains uncertainty and ownership.

Use explicit sockets and `-N` for borrowed tmux servers. Retiring a client
must not stop a borrowed server. Intentional server creation and server-owned
jobs need their own ownership boundaries.

## Building and distribution

Mix builds the shipped C source with a C11 compiler and Linux headers.
`CC` may name one compiler executable. Generated binaries are excluded from
Hex archives and rebuilt during dependency compilation. No third-party
runtime package or NIF is added.

Packed-core checks must compile and execute outside the checkout.
Workspace/MCP escript extraction and helper discovery still need their
installed-consumer checks; the current path expects an unpacked application
`priv` directory. Other platforms remain unqualified.

## Persistent connection components

The internal Guardian owns one native helper and monitors its Manager and
router independently. Startup grants one stdout credit after router demand.
After activation it keeps one native read in flight and buffers at most
64 KiB or 128 stdout chunks while Router consumes its previous chunk. Each
native read and delivered chunk fits 8 KiB. Exceeding either queue ceiling
closes the epoch with `resource_limit`; it does not indefinitely stop reading
from a still-attached client. These limits do not cap the borrowed tmux
server's allocations or total process memory.

Guardian caps stderr at 8 KiB and 64 chunks, and acknowledges one write
fragment at a time. A fragment fits 8 KiB; a complete rendered command fits
64 KiB. The writer rechecks the consumed publication lease, original deadline
and epoch. A partial line keeps its writer until the newline is acknowledged
or the epoch closes. Completed slots retain their generation to reject replay.

After orderly EOF or native exit, Guardian blocks further writes and drains
already-received stdout through the existing Router credits. An end token
follows pending native write acknowledgements; Router acknowledges it after
processing earlier data and write messages. Only then does ordinary closure
finalize remaining operations. Explicit closure, owner loss or protocol failure
can abort that drain. Established results survive; unfinished effects remain
uncertain. Drain and closure share the original 750 ms Guardian and 800 ms
Manager cleanup allowances. Neither clock restarts after data delivery.
Helper terminal acknowledgement remains independent of Router progress.

Deadline accounting uses one 25 ms timer, rescheduled only after consumption.
Busy delivery closes the epoch instead of suspending the owner or retrying.
Retirement needs native terminal proof, its acknowledgement and actual helper
exit; missing proof or Manager loss leaves the shared lifetime unclean.
Supervisor shutdown without those proofs also leaves it unclean.

Reserved closure revokes the exact lifetime generation without consuming a
command or metadata slot. Guardian observes that word on its accounting
timer even when Manager or Router makes no progress. A concurrent
starting-to-ready transition cannot escape revocation; retries follow only
the same generation. Revocation requests closure and blocks later checks.
It does not prove cleanup or prevent a write that already passed its final
check. Native and actor retirement remain separate required evidence.

Startup uses `attach-session -E` to preserve the borrowed session environment.
Attachment still changes client counts and session activity. After reading
the server PID and Linux process identity, a fresh same-connection challenge
must return the exact nonce/PID and receive a complete native write
acknowledgement before activation. It shares the original startup deadline.
The server and inspected `/proc` must share a PID namespace.

This requires host authority for completed, clean configuration throughout
the epoch: no aliases overriding admitted command names, no executable
effective hooks, and no unqualified messages or subscriptions that can write
to the control stream. Other clients can inject multiline text through
client-directed messages; parser limits cannot authenticate such output.
Absence of a configuration-error notification cannot certify configuration.
The library never silently disables hooks or changes configuration.

The internal epoch router registers operation identity and FIFO position
before sending fragments. A qualified reply after final-fragment dispatch
can establish an immutable logical result before the native acknowledgement
arrives. The writer still waits for native acknowledgement before advancing;
wire retirement also requires it. Completed reply events survive a later
parser error in the same chunk. Expired unsent work removes its exact queued
token before capacity reuse. A retained reply observation and its logical
result are separate copies in the eventual connection byte accounting.

The initial lane admits encoded field reads and literal server user-option
writes, with bounded ASCII option names and no value expansion. It rejects
arbitrary command lines. Literal send-keys still needs domain qualification:
pane-mode key bindings can enqueue additional commands even with `-l`.
Reply numbers must increase when observed; gaps are normal because other
clients and callbacks use the same server counter. This does not detect
every possible counter wrap or authenticate an unqualified stream.

Metadata requests use a separate fixed ETS inbox before any wake message.
Its context binds the real table owner, capacity, allowed request kinds and
atomics references. Publication creates the caller's reply alias and token;
only a small ready notification enters its mailbox. Owner completion and
caller receipt remain separate: a finished row stays occupied until alias
closure and receipt acknowledgement, or caller death. A monotone receipt
word cannot regress when a delayed old close meets a replacement generation.
Wake hints also coalesce across slot reuse; accounting sweeps never clear a
hint that a paused publisher still owns.

Inbox outcomes copy every binary leaf, including map keys. Copying charges
bytes and nodes before allocation, caps depth at64 and nodes at8192, and
rejects functions, ports and unqualified references. Known context references
come from explicitly identified, separately bounded resources. Metadata keeps
the default64 KiB outcome allowance; an independently configured Inbox may
reserve1–128 KiB so a64 KiB reply plus its envelope fits. The1 KiB minimum
covers fixed fallback errors. Copying shares the original deadline, checked
again before result publication. These limits do
not yet establish complete connection-wide heap/work accounting.

The selected waiter design retains bounded outcome copies in receipt-controlled
Inbox rows, superseding the earlier record-reference-only proposal. This avoids
cross-table pin/reclamation races at the cost of separately charged copies.
The internal waiter owner settles accepted requests from the exact immutable
terminal record before releasing it. A prior pending read cannot justify
forgetting a later completed record. Closed or expired waiters affect no
operation state; pre-acceptance await failures retain unknown effect certainty.
Manager services its separate waiter Inbox before reconnect admission and
startup continuations, and again after actor events. Both explicit forget
and automatic record expiry use the exact-record release barrier. A finished
waiter copy survives record reclamation and epoch replacement until receipt.
Lost waiter storage closes an active epoch and blocks this Manager's reuse.
If native retirement was already proved, that lifetime remains retired;
the Manager's fault does not erase cleanup knowledge or preserve lost tables
across its replacement.

Accounting finalizes retained records for all observed dead destinations in
one lease scan, matching each epoch and PID together. It preserves acknowledged
results and dispatched uncertainty, and releases no live destination's record.

`LibTmux.Operation` pins its original record, lease and Inboxes. Retained
status and result reads are local. Each await claims a bounded independent
slot and releases its exact alias and monitor on return; timeout does not
stop the operation. Metadata admission errors cannot label existing effects
as unwritten. Canonical failed, skipped and unknown outcomes remain values,
including in bang functions. Forget uses the original lease epoch after
reconnect. Stop validates the authoritative Births owner, epoch and Router
before revoking its generation through reserved capacity; an already-retired
record needs no surviving Births table. Stop closes the whole epoch and may
affect siblings. It is a request, never rollback or native retirement proof.

The retained-record registry finalizes an epoch only after its exact Router
PID has exited. It scans current admission leases, including a consumed
lease whose Router died before storing its first record. Router stores its
record and writing phase before sending, so an absent matching record proves
no write under that ordering. Existing acknowledged results remain intact;
dispatched work without evidence remains unknown. These outcomes retain
their slots until explicit release. Clearing a released record uses its
exact old value, preserving any replacement already published in that slot.
Logical finalization does not prove Guardian/helper cleanup or authorize a
new epoch; Manager must separately establish complete resource retirement.

Startup registration uses one fixed row for three epoch actor roles and its gate.
Each actor records its own PID before side effects. Closing the gate captures
all accepted PIDs in the same CAS; a queued late startup cannot be omitted
between a separate read and close. Router and Guardian bind the supplied
registration to their manager, epoch and original deadline. Guardian also
rechecks actor aliveness and its starting lifetime before opening the driver.
An accepted PID remains owned through actual exit: registration or a pre-open
check can race later closure. Gate closure alone is not native retirement.

Manager keeps one asynchronous request to an ordinary Supervisor outstanding
while it accounts for deadlines and metadata. A suspended Supervisor cannot
park that accounting. Closing the reply alias does not cancel a queued
Supervisor action; an abandoned unresolved start leaves cleanup unknown and
blocks replacement. Captured actors remain monitored independently of the
request alias. A Router born without a Guardian exits after the startup gate
closes. A captured pair binds even during closure, including buffered native
retirement events.

Explicit reconnect carries its original deadline through old retirement and
new bootstrap. Replacement requires native proof, actual Guardian and Router
exit, the host's child-finalization acknowledgment and EpochSupervisor exit.
Manager restarts preserve the external lifetime latch and do not reconnect
automatically. The internal qualified cases retain outcomes across reconnect,
forget exact completed leases, and expire retained records. Accepted metadata
work remains owned after caller timeout or alias closure; neither cancels it.

The internal connection Supervisor owns the view and starts EpochHost before
Manager. Its external child-spec factory pins the lifetime across root
restarts. Manager replacement invalidates its old tables; root replacement
also invalidates the view. A surviving view never recovers old operation
evidence. Finite Supervisor shutdown can leave descendants alive; only the
shared unknown/unretired lifetime prevents a replacement helper in that case.
An unsuccessful descriptor handoff after root startup kills the known root
and reports cleanup uncertainty, even after observing root exit.

The internal startup adapter passes the remaining initialization budget to
OTP's generic server entry with its source-qualified Supervisor init shape.
OTP stores the adapter as its callback; the adapter delegates the original
module and arguments. A private alias captures the exact Root PID before
delegation so cleanup drains only that Root's racing startup ACK or NACK.
Descriptor publication rechecks the original deadline, and failed handoff
cleanup uses only its remaining budget. OTP still waits for actual Root DOWN
after an initialization timeout; this primitive alone does not prove a strict
caller-return deadline or complete descendant retirement.

Both startup wrappers close their private reply aliases through local BIFs
and zero-time receives. Timeout cleanup does not demand-load the shared reply
helper after Root exit. Isolated loader-gate checks qualify this dependency;
they do not bound OTP's actual-DOWN wait or explain earlier timing failures.

Failed initial startup fences the fresh lifetime even before its first epoch
reservation. If that reservation wins the CAS race, the fence closes only the
first generation. Proven retirement remains intact, and later generations
cannot be revoked by an old failure. Root cleanup uses its generation captured
at startup entry. Manager can remain inert at generation zero with unknown
cleanup through normal shutdown or Host loss, without creating epoch actors.
This fence handles observed startup failures; it does not establish recovery
from untrappable caller or VM death. One lifetime belongs to one connection
Root; concurrent starts sharing that lifetime intentionally fail closed.

`Control.start_link/1` requires an explicit Server, exact existing session ID
and host-qualified lane. It returns `{:ok, root, control}` only after fresh
bootstrap and a bounded ready exchange. Its 1..600000ms timeout includes
preparation, Root startup and handoff; every successful handoff rechecks the
original deadline. The provisional handle stays internal. Accepted ready
replies bind their exact endpoint without a later Births or latest-view lookup.
If startup failed before ready registration, the error retains the original
failure kind. Cleanup fences the lifetime, requests exact-Root termination,
and reports actual Root exit only when observed. Native cleanup can remain
unknown. Ordinary linked-process exits retain their OTP semantics.

`Control.child_spec/1` prepares detached bounded process bytes without I/O.
One lifetime survives its permanent factory's invocations. Each invocation
starts a new startup budget, but a nonfresh lifetime returns inert instead of
automatically attaching. Explicit reconnect requires proven retirement;
unknown cleanup, including generation zero, returns a structured error.
`Supervisor.start_child/2` and `Supervisor.restart_child/2` return fresh handle
info. After automatic restart, terminate and restart that exact child to obtain
the new info; this recovery does not clear unknown cleanup. Retain a distinct
child spec/lifetime per Root, and never use an old handle as a locator.

`Control.submit/3` pins a ready Root view, Manager and epoch. It detaches the
request's binary leaves under a separate 20,000-byte owned-term limit before
claiming a fixed operation slot. One deadline includes validation, admission,
queueing, writing and replies. After claim, pure Operation binding preserves
the handle even if context disappears. A final local gate check can suppress
publication; the reserved lease stays owned. Its original deadline requests
epoch closure; capacity still follows native/destination retirement and
record retention or explicit forget rules. Router and Guardian independently
validate before writing.

`Control.request_close/1` requests whole-epoch closure without claiming a
slot, including when operation and metadata capacity are full. It does not
acknowledge native retirement or roll back siblings. Repeated requests for
the same closing or proven-retired generation succeed; old handles cannot
follow replacement Managers or epochs. Status errors report unknown
certainty about existing work; a rejected new, unadmitted submission reports
no write.

`Control.close/2` waits for native and epoch-actor retirement plus the Host's
epoch-child finalization acknowledgement under its original budget. An
admitted metadata watcher retains its fixed Inbox cell
through settlement, including after caller closure. Metadata settlement
failure blocks replacement. Ready watches never start a failed or closed
epoch. Accepted retirement watches settle before reconnect in the same batch,
independent of slot order. Epoch reservation rechecks metadata and waiter
storage; lost storage cannot authorize replacement.

`Control.reconnect/2` returns the acknowledged endpoint directly. A delayed
caller receives that epoch even if a newer one already exists; its handle
then reports stale. It does not reread the latest view or replay operations.
The Root and retained records outlive ordinary epoch closure. Public lifecycle
errors preserve unknown certainty about existing effects; direct retirement
proof must still be observed within the original close budget.

Strict caller-return startup bounds, connection-wide accounting and
authoritative subscriptions remain unqualified. These component checks do
not qualify those contracts.

# Command and field encoding

`LibTmux.Command` is a value. Constructing it or rendering its bytes performs
no I/O. The one-shot and control transports remain under implementation.

## Separate parsers

`Command.argv/2` returns process arguments and protects terminal semicolons
from tmux's argument-vector parser. It does not invoke a shell.
`Command.render/2` produces one tmux command line with every argument byte
octal-escaped inside double quotes. The result contains no raw newline or
carriage return. It excludes the framing newline a future writer must add.
Both renderers validate the encoded byte budget before dispatch.

Command quoting does not protect a value that a command interprets as a
tmux format. `LibTmux.Format.literal/1` constructs a literal format operand
without evaluating embedded `#{...}`, shell jobs or shorthand variables.
It accepts non-NUL bytes. The command still needs its own appropriate
format flags; arbitrary commands have different expansion behavior.

## One field per response

`Format.field/1` encodes a named field with a `v1:` marker. It replaces
backslashes first, then dollars and ASCII control bytes, using fixed tmux
substitutions. `LibTmux.Codec.decode_field/3` with `encoding: :escaped_v1`
requires that marker, removes one framing newline and decodes escapes once.
The conservative format performs several substitutions; it makes no
zero-copy or optimized multi-field claim.

This encoding avoids an ambiguity in tmux 3.4: its command print path
escapes some bytes while preserving literal backslashes. Removing arbitrary
backslashes from that output would corrupt legitimate values. A versioned
field encoding protects those values before printing. A separator byte
alone cannot do that, because titles and paths may contain it.

The default raw decoder removes only the final framing newline. Its source
must independently guarantee unmodified bytes. It must not be applied to
an unqualified tmux print path. Text decoding requires UTF-8; `:bytes`
retains arbitrary bytes. Integer parsing consumes the whole value and can
enforce a range; Boolean parsing accepts only `0` or `1`.

## Bounded framing

`LibTmux.Protocol` is a pure control-mode parser with separate chunk, line,
frame, line-count and emitted-event ceilings. It retains reply guard IDs;
notification-looking lines inside a reply remain output. A rejected suffix
preserves completed prefix events in the structured error. Retire a lane
after a parse error.

Lexical parsing cannot authenticate output that forges a matching guard.
Commands, aliases, hooks and subscriptions require separate admission
rules before sharing a persistent lane. Parser ceilings also do not bound
upstream Port delivery or a connection owner's mailbox. Those transport
contracts require independent qualification.
